# AI Will Affect Everyone's Future. Its Governance Can't Belong to a Few.

*Rebecca Finlay is CEO of the Partnership on AI.*

Members of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. [Source](https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en)

When world leaders gathered for last month's G7, the [image](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/20/ai-tech-moguls-g7) of a table set for heads of state and tech CEOs with the rest of the world looking on was striking. The future of AI, it seemed, was a conversation between the powerful and the more powerful.

Today offered a different picture. The [UN's Scientific Panel on AI](https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en?_gl=1*1hbyyns*_ga*MTU2NjA5MjM1MS4xNzgyNDExNTc3*_ga_S5EKZKSB78*czE3ODI5MTM0NzMkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODI5MTM0NzMkajYwJGwwJGgw)—established by resolution of all 193 UN member states and comprising 40 researchers from across disciplines and regions released the first assessment of AI and its implications for humanity.

That contrast points to a choice about who gets to set the terms for a technology that affects all of our lives. Governance can be shaped behind closed doors, or we can build the independent, international scientific foundation that policymakers and citizens everywhere need to define responsible AI in the public interest.

Shared scientific foundations are what makes durable action possible. Aviation became the world's safest form of transport because governments chose to build it together. In 1944, they established ICAO, the UN agency that replaced a patchwork of fragmented national rules with a single global framework, contributing to a dramatic decline in accident rates worldwide over time.

Next week's inaugural [UN Global Dialogue on AI](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en) in Geneva marks a similar opportunity to create a shared foundation that travels across borders.

Investing in building an international scientific consensus is an important first step. Rigorous analysis produces findings that can be tested and challenged. But rigor alone is not enough. Science also needs to be transparent, in that it is published, debated, scrutinized, and revised.

That's how science works. It isn't perfect, but it doesn't have to be.

CERN (the [European Organization for Nuclear Research](https://home.cern/)) has spent seven decades showing what is possible when nations choose shared scientific infrastructure over national competition.

Across the board, policymakers are having to make consequential decisions about AI policy with limited transparency and a lack of verified measurements, evaluations and technical standards. It is as if we are regulating road safety without agreed speed limits, crash tests, or even a shared basic definition of what a car is.

#### Our content delivered to your inbox.

#### Thank you!

The public is also concerned, as anxiety about the effects of AI on work and communities are rising.

How then do we lay the groundwork for international action starting with Geneva? As co-lead of the Safe, Secure and Trustworthy AI session, I firmly believe one measure of success is whether Geneva leaves us with a shared commitment to rigorous, inclusive scientific consensus-building. That means three things.

First, building coherence across efforts that have been largely moving in isolation, such as the UK-funded [State of AI Safety report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/), the Singapore [Consensus on AI Safety Research Priorities](https://www.scai.gov.sg/2025/scai2025-report/), and the forthcoming [Global South State of AI Safety Report](https://www.digitalfutureslab.in/news/an-ai-safety-report-for-the-global-south-by-the-global-south).

The UN Scientific Panel and the UN Global Dialogue are designed to work together. The Panel builds the evidence base, and the Dialogue is the mechanism for translating that evidence into direction for policymakers. Done well, a clear roadmap coming out of the Dialogue’s can be the connective tissue that binds all of these efforts into a shared foundation.

Second, strengthening the institutions already doing the evaluation work. The [International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/international-ai-network-consensus-and-open-questions) represents one of the most tangible policy innovations of the AI Summit Series. Linking the work of the institutes with the UN Scientific Panel creates an opportunity to define what we measure, and how we measure, through a more global understanding of responsible AI.

Third, committing to building the infrastructure to advance open science. Consequential breakthroughs in human history, including the human genome, climate models, and protein structures, happened when research was done openly. Transparency doesn't slow progress. It is what makes progress verifiable, credible, and worth defending.

Geneva offers the governments, scientists, and civil society organisations gathered this week the opportunity to turn responsible AI from a catchphrase into a roadmap people can see, measure, and hold us to. The UN is not a perfect institution, but no other body brings the international reach to answer this question.

As AI is rapidly reshaping our workplaces, our schools, and our homes, we still have time to shape it in return. After many years working at the intersection of AI and public interest, I believe that AI will only go as far as trust takes it — and trust is built on clarity, evidence, and knowledge shared openly.

# AI 將影響每個人的未來。它的治理不能由少數人掌握。

*Rebecca Finlay 是 Partnership on AI 執行長。*

聯合國 AI 獨立國際科學小組成員。[來源](https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en)

上個月世界領袖齊聚 G7 時，那張為國家元首與科技公司執行長擺好的餐桌、其餘世界只能旁觀的[畫面](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/20/ai-tech-moguls-g7)格外醒目。AI 的未來，看起來像是有權者與更有權者之間的對話。

今天呈現了不同的景象。[聯合國 AI 科學小組](https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en?_gl=1*1hbyyns*_ga*MTU2NjA5MjM1MS4xNzgyNDExNTc3*_ga_S5EKZKSB78*czE3ODI5MTM0NzMkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODI5MTM0NzMkajYwJGwwJGgw)由 193 個聯合國會員國共同決議成立，成員包括來自不同學科與地區的 40 位研究者；該小組發布了首份關於 AI 及其對人類影響的評估報告。

這樣的對比，指向一個選擇：究竟誰有資格為一項影響我們所有人生活的技術設定規則。治理可以在閉門之後成形；或者，我們也可以建立獨立、國際性的科學基礎，讓各地的政策制定者與公民，都能據此從公共利益出發，定義負責任的 AI。

共享的科學基礎，正是讓持久行動成為可能的原因。航空之所以成為全世界最安全的交通形式，是因為各國政府選擇共同打造它。1944 年，各國成立了 ICAO 這個聯合國專門機構，以單一全球架構取代破碎分散的各國規則，並隨著時間推移，促成全球事故率大幅下降。

下週將在日內瓦首次舉行的[聯合國 AI 全球對話](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en)，標誌著一個類似的機會：建立一套能跨越國界的共享基礎。

投資建立國際科學共識，是重要的第一步。嚴謹的分析會產生可以被檢驗與挑戰的發現。但光有嚴謹還不夠。科學也需要透明，也就是要被公開發表、辯論、檢視與修正。

這就是科學運作的方式。它並不完美，但也不需要完美。

CERN（[歐洲核子研究組織](https://home.cern/)）七十年來持續展現，當各國選擇共享科學基礎建設，而不是國家競爭時，能夠實現什麼可能。

整體而言，政策制定者正被迫在透明度有限、缺乏經驗證的量測、評估與技術標準的情況下，對 AI 政策做出影響深遠的決定。這就像是在沒有共同認可的速限、撞擊測試，甚至連「車」是什麼都沒有基本共同定義的情況下，規範道路安全。

#### 將我們的內容送到你的信箱。

#### 謝謝！

公眾同樣感到憂心，因為人們對 AI 影響工作與社群的焦慮正在升高。

那麼，我們該如何從日內瓦開始，為國際行動奠定基礎？身為「安全、可靠且可信賴 AI」場次的共同主持人，我堅信，衡量成功的一項標準，是日內瓦是否能讓我們共同承諾，投入嚴謹且具包容性的科學共識建構。這代表三件事。

第一，讓各項大多各自推進的努力彼此銜接，例如英國資助的 [AI 安全現況報告](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/)、新加坡的 [AI 安全研究優先事項共識](https://www.scai.gov.sg/2025/scai2025-report/)，以及即將發布的[全球南方 AI 安全現況報告](https://www.digitalfutureslab.in/news/an-ai-safety-report-for-the-global-south-by-the-global-south)。

聯合國科學小組與聯合國全球對話的設計，本來就是要相互配合。小組建立證據基礎，而對話則是把這些證據轉化為政策制定者方向的機制。若執行得當，對話產出的清楚路線圖，可以成為把所有這些努力連結成共同基礎的結締組織。

第二，強化那些已經在進行評估工作的機構。[先進 AI 量測、評估與科學國際網絡](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/international-ai-network-consensus-and-open-questions) 是 AI 高峰會系列中最具體的政策創新之一。把各研究機構的工作與聯合國科學小組連結起來，將創造一個機會，透過更全球性的負責任 AI 理解，界定我們要量測什麼，以及如何量測。

第三，承諾打造推進開放科學的基礎建設。人類歷史上影響深遠的突破，包括人類基因組、氣候模型與蛋白質結構，都是在研究以開放方式進行時發生的。透明不會拖慢進展；正是透明，讓進展可被驗證、值得信任，也值得捍衛。

日內瓦為本週聚集於此的各國政府、科學家與公民社會組織，提供了一個機會，把負責任 AI 從口號變成一張人人看得見、可以衡量、也能據以要求我們負責的路線圖。聯合國不是完美的機構，但沒有其他組織具備同樣的國際觸及能力，能夠回應這個問題。

隨著 AI 正快速重塑我們的工作場域、學校與家庭，我們仍有時間反過來形塑它。在 AI 與公共利益交會處工作多年後，我相信 AI 能走多遠，只取決於信任能帶它走多遠；而信任建立在清楚明確、證據，以及公開分享的知識之上。
